conceptTag: Why Facebook started with one campus
readerTitle: Why Facebook started with one campus, not the whole internet
caseNote: 실제 기업 (Facebook 초기 대학별 확장, 2004~2006) + 실제 관찰 (도시별로 출시하는 차량 호출 서비스) + 가상 적용 (B2B 구매 담당자 네트워크)
insight: 네트워크의 가치는 전체 사용자 수가 아니라 내 사람들이 얼마나 촘촘히 모여 있느냐에서 나온다. 그래서 작은 집단 하나를 먼저 꽉 채우는 것이 빠른 길이다.
misconception: 네트워크 효과가 있는 사업은 처음부터 최대한 넓게 열어 사용자 수를 늘려야 이긴다.

sources.text: The Harvard Crimson, 2004년 2월 TheFacebook 출시 보도 (harvard.edu 이메일 가입 조건, 초기 가입 속도)
Kirkpatrick, D. (2010). The Facebook Effect. Simon & Schuster. (대학별 확장, 고등학교 개방, 2006년 일반 공개)
Facebook 2006년 9월 일반 공개 발표 (13세 이상, 유효한 이메일 보유자)

factChecks.note: 출시일 2004년 2월 4일, harvard.edu 이메일 필요 조건은 Meta 연혁과 Harvard Crimson 보도로 확인하세요.
2004년 3월 Columbia, Stanford, Yale로 확장했다는 내용은 여러 자료에 나오지만 순서와 날짜를 게시 전 확인하세요. 카드에는 학교 이름과 'March 2004'만 적었습니다.
초기 하버드 가입 비율(한 달 안에 학부생 절반 이상 등)은 자료마다 수치가 달라 카드에는 'a large share within weeks'로만 적었습니다.
고등학교 개방(2005년 9월)과 일반 공개(2006년 9월 26일) 날짜를 Facebook 발표 자료로 확인하세요. 카드에는 연도와 월 수준으로만 적었습니다.
차량 호출 서비스가 도시별로 출시한다는 내용은 일반적인 관찰로만 적었고 특정 회사 수치는 쓰지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Why Facebook started with one campus, not the whole internet
body: In February 2004, a student website called TheFacebook went live. You could only join with a harvard.edu email address.
Everyone else was locked out. That gate looked like a limit. It turned out to be the growth plan.

image.label: A single glowing campus on a dark map
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 어두운 지도 위에 대학 캠퍼스 하나만 밝게 빛나고, 캠퍼스 안 작은 사람들이 선으로 촘촘히 연결됨. 바깥은 비어 있음. 실제 로고, 학교 문장, 브랜드 색은 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Your site is a hit on one campus. What next?
body: It's spring 2004. Within weeks, a large share of students at your university have signed up. Students at other schools are asking to join, and you could open the doors tomorrow.

options.text: Open to anyone with an email address, anywhere
options.feedback: You'd grow the total count fast, but most newcomers would find almost no one they know. A big, thin network feels empty to each person in it.

options.text: Add campuses one at a time, each as its own closed group
options.feedback: Growth is slower on paper, but each new school can fill up quickly with people who already know each other. This is roughly what Facebook did.

options.text: Open to every college in the country at once
options.feedback: Keeping it to students protects the feel of the site. But launching everywhere at once spreads your attention thin and leaves many campuses half-empty.

cards.title: One gate at a time.
body: Each step opened a new group that was dense on its own: people who already knew each other, joining together.

breakdown.label: High schools
breakdown.detail: A new set of tight groups

cards.title: Density beats size
body: With **local network effects**, a network's value to you depends on how many of *your* people are on it, not how many people are on it in total.
A site with 2,000 of your classmates beats a site with a million strangers. So the smart early goal is not the biggest network. It's a small one where nearly everyone you care about is already there.

image.label: Small dense cluster vs large scattered crowd
image.brief: 두 그림 나란히 비교. 왼쪽: 작은 원 안에 점 20개가 거의 모두 선으로 연결됨 ("Small, dense"). 오른쪽: 넓은 화면에 점 200개가 흩어져 있고 연결선은 몇 개뿐 ("Big, thin"). 왼쪽이 더 따뜻한 색.

cards.title: Why one campus was the right size.
body: A single university gave the early site several things at once.
list: **A closed group:** classmates, dorms and clubs already linked people
**Real identities:** a school email meant profiles were real students
**Reachable critical mass:** filling one campus is far easier than filling a country
**A repeatable launch:** each new school started as its own dense group
cards.callout: The gate didn't slow growth. It made each step of growth stick.

cards.title: The same logic shows up offline.
body: Many ride-hailing and delivery services launch city by city. A driver in another city does nothing for you, so each city has to fill up on its own.
A farmers market works the same way. Ten stalls in one square on Saturday morning draw a crowd. The same ten stalls spread across town on different days draw almost no one.
When value comes from who's nearby, start where you can be dense.

cards.title: Small and dense isn't always the answer.
body: This works when people mostly want to reach others in their own group. If customers want reach across the whole market, such as buyers of rare parts searching worldwide, a tiny closed network may be too small to be useful.
Gates also have a cost. While you expand slowly, rivals can take the groups you haven't reached. And exclusivity has a shelf life: Facebook eventually opened to everyone.

cards.title: Now it's a network for buyers.
body: You're launching a members-only service where company purchasing managers share reviews of suppliers. Reviews are only useful if buyers in the same field contribute them.

options.text: Launch nationally to every industry with a big ad campaign
options.feedback: You'd get sign-ups, but a hospital buyer won't care about reviews of packaging suppliers. Each member would find too little that's relevant.

options.text: Start with hospital purchasing in one region until most of them take part
options.feedback: A small field where buyers share suppliers fills up fast and becomes useful quickly. You give up early reach to get a network that's actually worth joining.

options.text: Start with one industry, but nationwide
options.feedback: Better focus than A. But if suppliers differ by region, many members still won't see reviews of the firms they use.

cards.title: Win a small group completely before you go wide.
body: A network feels valuable when your people are already there. Fill one dense group, then copy the launch to the next.
**Try it today:** name the smallest group of customers who would get real value from each other. How close are you to reaching most of them?
